options.why: Uncertainty disclosure is not processing authorization.

options.text: Keep current analysis within approved issue trends; seek the responsible assessment before sensitive inference or secondary use.
options.why: The new purpose needs its own applicable assessment.

options.text: Proceed with sensitive inference because customers voluntarily supplied the conversations while seeking support for the original product issue.
options.why: Voluntary disclosure for support does not establish every secondary purpose.

options.text: Remove names but retain account identifiers, using inferred traits for targeting without secondary-purpose review.
options.why: Pseudonymization does not remove the new processing purpose.

questions.decision: A permitted data source does not authorize every inferred attribute or secondary use; preserve the approved purpose boundary.

questions.title: Discovery when users disagree on the baseline
questions.stem: A purchasing assistant pilot reports eight minutes saved per request. Experienced buyers say the baseline includes work they never perform; newer buyers say the new workflow omits mandatory checks. The sponsor wants to scale the pilot immediately. Success is defined as shorter fully compliant handling time. Which discovery step BEST resolves the evidence conflict before a rollout commitment?

options.text: Observe representative buyers, agree the complete compliant task baseline, and remeasure pilot effort including omitted checks.
options.why: The claimed benefit depends on a disputed task definition.

options.text: Retain the sponsor-approved baseline for simpler reporting, without checking disputed required work or buyer differences.
options.why: Convenient consistency does not validate the disputed measure.

options.text: Scale first and gather more satisfaction responses, treating increased sample size as sufficient to validate the existing time-saving claim.
options.why: More responses do not fix an invalid task boundary.

options.text: Average the two buyer groups' opinions and use that number as the new baseline without observing the actual required work.
options.why: Opinion averaging does not resolve omitted checks.

questions.decision: A business baseline must represent the full intended task and population before it can support a value or rollout claim.

questions.title: A decision communication that preserves uncertainty
questions.stem: A team selects regional processing because a documented residency requirement is satisfied there. A global endpoint is cheaper and scores better, but its terms for this workload remain unresolved. The sponsor understands that both quality and residency matter, yet asks for a clear decision record and future review condition. Which TWO communication elements BEST avoid both hiding trade-offs and treating unresolved terms as established facts?

options.text: Document the regional choice and its current cost but omit the higher-scoring alternative because reviewers cannot select it today.
options.why: That hides a material trade-off and future review option.

options.text: Record the global benchmark advantage as the release decision, postponing the residency question until after the preferred configuration is deployed.
options.why: This treats an unresolved feasibility condition as satisfied.

options.text: Record the selected option, responsible reviewer and specific residency evidence that would trigger reconsideration of the global alternative.
options.why: This creates an accountable conditional decision rather than a permanent claim.

options.text: State which requirements are verified, which remain unresolved and how the feasible options compare on measured quality and cost.
options.why: This separates known constraints from preferences and uncertainty.

options.text: Describe global processing as permanently prohibited without preserving the unresolved-term distinction, simplifying the decision into one universal legal rule.
options.why: The supplied uncertainty does not establish a universal prohibition.

questions.decision: A useful decision record distinguishes evidence, uncertainty and trade-offs, and says what would justify revisiting the choice.

questions.title: A fallback changes the service promise
questions.stem: A customer agreement promises a supported answer within four seconds. During dependency outages the team proposes returning an acknowledgment in one second and sending the answer later, while continuing to report every acknowledgment as SLA success. The fallback is useful but was not part of the agreed completion definition. Which next action BEST aligns expectations and monitoring before enabling it broadly?

options.text: Enable the fallback and count acknowledgments as completed supported answers because the user receives some response within the existing target.
options.why: That silently changes the promised outcome.

options.text: Disable every acknowledgment during outages so users see no response until a supported answer meets the original four-second target.
options.why: Users can receive useful status without misreporting compliance.

options.text: Agree and instrument separate degraded acknowledgment and eventual-answer commitments, keeping original completion breaches visible pending accepted changes.
options.why: A useful fallback requires explicit service semantics.

options.text: Exclude all dependency-outage requests from reporting without customer agreement, preserving a favorable normal-operation latency chart.
options.why: Unagreed exclusions do not align the service obligation.

questions.decision: A fallback can be valuable without satisfying the original SLA; make its separate commitment explicit rather than relabeling success.

questions.title: Implementation guidance after an ownership split
questions.stem: A delivery team builds an assistant while another team owns retrieval indexing. Incidents repeatedly bounce between them because the handoff says only that search is integrated. Both components meet isolated tests, but nobody owns stale-source detection or reindex rollback. Which TWO documentation changes BEST address this cross-team gap rather than merely adding more component diagrams?

options.text: Keep ownership informal until incident volume is high enough to justify a separate cross-team project.
options.why: The recurring operational gap is already established.

options.text: Add a detailed diagram of each team's internal classes without defining which team acts when the integrated answer uses stale evidence.
options.why: Internal diagrams do not resolve boundary ownership.

options.text: Specify version compatibility, failure signals and a tested reindex/rollback procedure that both teams exercise during handoff.
options.why: This makes operational coordination implementable and verifiable.

options.text: Document end-to-end freshness and recovery responsibilities with named owners, escalation paths and joint acceptance criteria at the retrieval boundary.
options.why: This assigns the unowned cross-component behavior.

options.text: Assign every stale-answer incident to the model team by default because it produces the final prose, regardless of upstream source state.
options.why: The default ignores actual failure responsibility and repair authority.

questions.decision: Document shared service behavior and decision ownership at interfaces; isolated component acceptance cannot establish end-to-end operability.

questions.title: A loud request versus representative feedback
questions.stem: A major customer requests a much longer answer format. Smaller customers say the current concise format is essential, and support data shows different needs by task type. The product owner wants a single immediate global prompt change to satisfy the largest account. Which response BEST handles feedback while preserving evidence-based product behavior and existing commitments?

options.text: Apply the largest customer's preferred format globally, treating commercial priority as evidence of universal task fit.
options.why: Commercial priority does not establish every user's task need.

options.text: Let the model infer customer importance from query wording and silently vary detail without a documented product configuration or evaluation.
options.why: Implicit untested variation is difficult to govern or explain.

options.text: Reject the request because the original concise format passed acceptance and therefore cannot be revised after launch.
options.why: Accepted behavior can evolve through controlled change.

options.text: Clarify task-specific needs, test approved format variants on affected slices, and agree explicit configuration and ownership.
options.why: This addresses real differences without assuming one account represents all users.

questions.decision: Feedback should be translated into explicit user/task requirements and evaluated options, not weighted solely by the loudest source.

questions.title: A prototype cannot answer a rollout-capacity question
questions.stem: A successful analyst pilot uses a curated document collection and a dedicated support engineer. A planned enterprise rollout adds forty departments with independent retention rules and no assigned support capacity. Executives ask for a delivery estimate based on the pilot's two-week build. Which next step BEST supports a defensible estimate without discarding the pilot's useful technical evidence?

options.text: Discover departmental requirements and rollout ownership, then estimate staged delivery with explicit dependencies, assumptions and validation effort.
options.why: The pilot omits material rollout scope and support obligations.

options.text: Reuse the two-week estimate unchanged because the core model interaction already demonstrated technical feasibility on curated documents.
options.why: Technical feasibility does not establish enterprise readiness.

options.text: Restart all prototype engineering from scratch before interviewing departments, assuming nothing from a small pilot can inform a larger program.
options.why: The pilot's validated technical findings remain useful.

options.text: Multiply the pilot build time by forty and present the result as a complete enterprise implementation estimate without further discovery.
options.why: Linear scaling ignores shared work and new constraints.

questions.decision: Reuse evidence within its scope while discovering new rollout requirements; an estimate must include the changed operating model.

questions.title: An iteration proposal ready for a governance forum
questions.stem: Monitoring reveals that a document assistant underperforms on a newly common source format. A repair requires a parser change, not a model upgrade. The steering group needs to approve effort and understand user impact; operations needs a rollback plan. Which THREE elements BEST make the proposal concrete enough for both an informed decision and controlled implementation?

options.text: Specify staged rollout, monitoring triggers and rollback responsibility, communicating expected temporary limitations to affected service owners.
options.why: This makes the release operable and expectations explicit.

options.text: Show the affected workload share and supported failure evidence, distinguishing business impact from unrelated aggregate model benchmarks.
options.why: This establishes why the iteration matters.

options.text: Present only a favorable demonstration on one repaired document, leaving affected traffic, interface changes and recovery ownership for later.
options.why: One example does not support the delivery and operating decision.

options.text: Request a blanket model-upgrade budget because all assistant failures can be categorized as insufficient language-model capability.
options.why: It does not address the diagnosed parser defect.

options.text: Describe the parser change, interfaces, owner and representative acceptance tests, including regressions against existing document formats.
options.why: This defines implementable scope and verification.

questions.decision: An iteration proposal should connect observed impact, bounded repair and release control; diagnosis determines the work rather than AI branding.

questions.title: Retiring an assistant with active obligations
questions.stem: A company will retire an old procurement assistant after replacing it. The old system still has pending approvals, scheduled notifications and links in active cases. Operations proposes turning off the endpoint immediately because new questions already use the replacement. Which lifecycle plan BEST retires the service without abandoning users or executing stale pending work?

options.text: Reconcile outstanding obligations with owners, migrate or close them, communicate access changes, and verify pending effects and credentials are retired.
options.why: Retirement must account for active state and authority.

options.text: Delete the old database immediately because no new questions are routed there, assuming pending approvals belong to the replacement automatically.
options.why: Routing new traffic does not migrate existing obligations.

options.text: Keep the old service fully privileged indefinitely so historical links work without explicit migration decisions.
options.why: Indefinite authority is unnecessary and complicates ownership.

options.text: Stop the endpoint immediately and leave pending jobs running on their existing credentials until users report any missing results.
options.why: This leaves unowned effects and abandoned cases.

questions.decision: Lifecycle management includes retirement and reconciliation of active commitments, not only launch and prompt iteration.

questions.title: A missed commitment and an honest recovery plan
questions.stem: A team committed to a launch date before discovering that a third-party connector lacks required audit metadata. The missing control blocks the approved production scope; a read-only limited pilot remains feasible. The sponsor asks the architect to maintain the date by describing the gap as post-launch cleanup. Which TWO responses BEST preserve expectation alignment and an actionable delivery decision?

options.text: Describe the limited pilot as the full production release so the date remains unchanged, then expand silently when the connector is repaired.
options.why: That misaligns stakeholder expectations and scope.

options.text: Launch the original scope and record the audit-metadata gap only in an internal backlog, retaining the original readiness announcement.
options.why: It hides a known unmet acceptance condition.

options.text: Explain the blocked acceptance condition, impact and evidence promptly, separating the original production commitment from the feasible limited pilot.
options.why: This prevents an undisclosed change to readiness claims.

options.text: Cancel the entire program without offering the feasible pilot or explaining which constraint caused the production delay.
options.why: It removes an available informed option.

options.text: Present revised scope/date options with owners and dependencies, obtaining an explicit decision and updating acceptance and operational communication accordingly.
options.why: The recovery becomes a concrete agreed delivery plan.

questions.decision: Surface the unmet commitment with feasible choices; honest scope and dependency communication is part of architectural delivery.

questions.title: Formatter feedback within the editing loop
questions.stem: A team already has a deterministic repository formatter and CI validation. Developers want immediate formatting feedback after AI source edits, before review; commit and deployment remain separate approved steps. Prompt reminders are often missed. The project formatter supports a bounded modified-file invocation. Which configuration BEST reuses the existing tool at the requested point without expanding the workflow's action scope?

options.text: Run a formatter hook that silently ignores failures, relying on CI to detect whether the immediate formatting action actually succeeded.
options.why: The immediate feedback is misleading when the formatter fails.

options.text: Run the repository formatter on modified files through a scoped edit hook, surface failures and retain CI validation.
options.why: It gives immediate deterministic feedback with bounded effects.

options.text: Run a full-repository formatter after every edit and silently rewrite unrelated generated files before the review starts.
options.why: It expands the change scope beyond the supported modified-file action.

options.text: Keep formatting only in CI after pull-request submission, preserving deterministic checks but providing no edit-loop feedback.
options.why: It misses the requested timing despite useful later validation.

questions.decision: Reuse the deterministic tool at the needed feedback point, limiting effects and exposing errors instead of adding unrelated automation.

questions.title: An AI debug assistant that needs observability
questions.stem: Developers repeatedly paste partial error messages into a coding assistant. It proposes plausible fixes, but many fail because the actual configuration and failing test command are missing. The repository already has reproducible test scripts and sanitized diagnostic logs. The team wants shorter debugging cycles while keeping human review. Which TWO workflow changes BEST improve the evidence available to the assistant?

options.text: Provide the exact failing command, relevant sanitized trace, environment version and minimal reproduction before asking for a repair hypothesis.
options.why: This grounds diagnosis in the actual failure conditions.

options.text: Paste full environment dumps including secrets so the assistant can infer every possible configuration detail without a scoping step.
options.why: This exposes sensitive data unnecessarily.

options.text: Have the assistant validate a bounded proposed change with the existing relevant test, recording what passed and retaining review of the resulting diff.
options.why: This closes the diagnosis-to-verification loop.

options.text: Disable the failing test until the proposed repair is merged, using a successful build as proof the original runtime error is resolved.
options.why: A different passing check does not validate the failed behavior.

options.text: Ask the assistant for more speculative fixes per error and merge the first one that reads convincingly to an unfamiliar reviewer.
options.why: More guesses do not replace missing evidence.

questions.decision: Better debugging assistance comes from reproducible evidence and targeted verification, not the volume of plausible patches.

questions.title: A permission denial is not a broken tool
questions.stem: A coding assistant's build command works locally but is denied in the shared execution environment. The denial message identifies a prohibited network access, while the project also supports an offline dependency cache. The team must retain the approved execution policy. Which diagnostic response BEST distinguishes policy from tool failure and finds a permitted verification path?

options.text: Report the build passed from local behavior, omitting the shared environment's unexecuted verification and denial.
options.why: That misstates the evidence actually obtained.

options.text: Disable the shared execution policy temporarily because a command that works locally proves the denial is a tool defect.
options.why: Local success does not authorize prohibited access.

options.text: Inspect the denied capability, test the approved offline-cache build path, and report any remaining verification limits precisely.
options.why: This respects policy while testing an available permitted path.

options.text: Retry the same networked build repeatedly with different wording in the assistant prompt until the denial no longer appears.
options.why: Prompt wording does not address the policy boundary.

questions.decision: A denied capability and an implementation error require different responses; use permitted alternatives and state verification limits honestly.

questions.title: A changed tool interface after an upgrade
questions.stem: A team upgrades its approved MCP server. Existing prompts still name an old tool and assume a field that the new schema removed. The server is reachable and authentication succeeds; calls fail validation before execution. The team needs a repeatable repair across developers without weakening the server's schema checks. Which TWO changes BEST address the actual compatibility failure?

options.text: Refresh credentials repeatedly because successful authentication can still be the most likely cause of a deterministic schema-validation error.
options.why: The observed failure already identifies the incompatible request.

options.text: Add a small compatibility smoke test for the required operation and distribute the corrected shared configuration through the established team setup.
options.why: This catches and consistently propagates the repaired contract.

options.text: Ask each developer to invent local aliases for the removed tool and omit documenting the server version to avoid coupling.
options.why: Untracked aliases create more divergent interfaces.

options.text: Disable argument validation on the server so prompts written against the removed field can continue sending their previous request shapes.
options.why: Weakening validation does not restore intended operation semantics.

options.text: Compare the pinned client expectations with the server's current advertised tools and schemas, updating the integration contract and version compatibility record.
options.why: The error concerns interface mismatch rather than connectivity.

questions.decision: Localize failures by boundary; reachable authenticated servers can still reject an outdated caller contract.

drills.title: Validity of evidence and measurement
drills.stem: Judge each row independently against its stated requirement. Choose Yes or No for each; no fixed number of Yes answers is implied.

rows.text: Requirement: estimate single-run agent reliability. Evidence: every task succeeded at least once across five attempts, with failed attempts omitted.
rows.why: Existence of a successful attempt is not single-run reliability.

rows.text: Requirement: evaluate a repair task repeatedly. Proposal: reset each trial to known state and grade the required outcome plus forbidden side effects.
rows.why: Controlled starting conditions and behavior criteria support valid repeated trials.

rows.text: Requirement: answer historical ownership. Proposal: retrieve current ownership summaries and always prefer the newest document.
rows.why: Current ownership does not establish the relation at the requested historical date.

rows.text: Requirement: preserve units in retrieved evidence. Proposal: index table rows with their associated headers, units and provenance.
rows.why: The source structure carries meaning essential to the number.

rows.text: Requirement: understand dialect quality disparity. Proposal: revalidate disputed labels with qualified reviewers before drawing system fairness conclusions.
rows.why: The measurement process must be valid before interpreting the gap.

drills.title: Boundaries during change
drills.stem: Judge each row independently against its stated requirement. Choose Yes or No for each; no fixed number of Yes answers is implied.

rows.text: Requirement: retain a fixed investigation budget. Proposal: every worker has a local cap, but replacement workers can be spawned without a shared cap.
rows.why: Unlimited replacement delegation can exceed the authorized aggregate budget.

rows.text: Requirement: useful service during an outage. Proposal: offer an explicit pending acknowledgment while continuing to count unfulfilled original completion promises accurately.
rows.why: Useful status and honest completion measurement can coexist.

rows.text: Requirement: safe retirement. Proposal: reconcile pending approvals and scheduled effects before revoking credentials and closing the old service.
rows.why: Outstanding obligations need deliberate transfer or closure.

rows.text: Requirement: enforce tenant search permissions. Proposal: authenticate page one only and allow arbitrary offsets for later pages.
rows.why: Every data-returning page remains an authorization boundary.

rows.text: Requirement: bounded formatting automation. Proposal: a formatter hook also commits and deploys every edit without separate review.
rows.why: The extra effects exceed the requested deterministic formatting action.

drills.title: Locate the failing boundary
drills.stem: Choose the BEST primary boundary to investigate for each observation. Options may repeat; these are practice categories, not a live-exam format guarantee.

rows.text: A quality score rises after abstentions because the dashboard now excludes unanswered cases from its denominator.
rows.why: The measurement changed what success means.

rows.text: The correct table row is retrieved, but its unit and heading were dropped during ingestion.
rows.why: The source structure lost essential meaning before generation.

rows.text: A reachable authenticated MCP server rejects a removed argument field after an upgrade.
rows.why: Caller and server schema expectations no longer match.

rows.text: A retired service still holds scheduled notifications and pending approvals with active credentials.
rows.why: Retirement did not reconcile active commitments and effects.

rows.text: New query embeddings search a collection mixing old and new incompatible document-vector representations.
rows.why: The retrieval representation is not version-consistent.
